requirements:
The system manages warehouse zone access and order picking.

The people involved are pickers, forklift operators, zone supervisors, warehouse managers, and security officers. One person may hold both the picker and the forklift operator role at the same time.

The resources are orders, which record who requested them, the picker, items, item count, pick list code, status, destination zone, and release time, and zones, which record zone code, sensitivity, zone group, whether the zone is locked, and operational status.

Each request carries the current time, whether the requester has badged in on-site for the shift, and whether an emergency has been declared.

A picker or forklift operator may pick an order only after they have badged in on-site for the shift.

A picker or forklift operator who has not badged in on-site for the shift may not pick an order.

Neither a picker nor a forklift operator may pick an order they requested themselves when the order's line-item count does not cross the bulk-pick threshold.

When the order's line-item count crosses the bulk-pick threshold, the picker or forklift operator who requested the order may pick it themselves.

A request by a picker to pick an order that does not trip any prohibition above must be able to succeed.

The system manages job applications, interview feedback, and offers for recruiting.

The people involved are recruiters, hiring managers, interviewers, and coordinators. One person may hold recruiter and interviewer roles together, or recruiter and hiring manager roles together.

The resources are applications, interview feedback, and offers, with each application recording its candidate, referrer, hiring team, req code, PII sensitivity, and status, each interview feedback record recording its application, interviewer, candidate, and status, and each offer recording its application, extender, compensation, signing bonus, and status.

Each person making a request carries their PII clearance.

Each request carries whether it is from the corporate network, the current time, and whether executive approval is present.

A hiring manager may approve an offer only while the offer is drafted, unless the request falls within a permitted window.

When the request falls within a permitted window, the hiring manager may approve an offer that is not drafted.

A hiring manager must not approve an offer that is not drafted when the request is outside the permitted window.

A request by a hiring manager to approve an offer that does not trip any prohibition above must be able to succeed.

The system manages the release of laboratory test results to patient charts in a hospital clinical lab.

The people involved are medical technologists, pathologists, ordering providers, and the lab director. One person may hold both the pathologist and ordering provider roles at the same time, and one person may hold both the medical technologist and pathologist roles at the same time.

The resources are lab results and lab orders. Every lab result records its patient, its ordering provider, the technologist who verified it, its sensitivity level, whether it carries a critical-value flag, the time it was released to the patient portal, and its status. Every lab order records its patient, its ordering provider, its test code, and its status.

Each request carries the current time, whether multi-factor authentication was used, whether the requester is on the hospital network, whether this is an emergency release, and whether coverage has been authorized.

A pathologist or an ordering provider may release a lab result.

The technologist who verified a lab result must not be the same person who releases it, even when that person also holds the pathologist role.

A pathologist or an ordering provider must not release a lab result that has not yet been verified.

When a lab result's sensitivity is at a restricted level, an ordering provider must not release it, and only a pathologist may do so.

For a restricted-sensitivity result that also carries a critical-value flag, an ordering provider may release it despite the restriction.

A request by a pathologist to release a verified result that does not trip any of the restrictions above must be able to succeed.

The system manages network change control approval and maintenance-window implementation at a telecommunications carrier.

The people involved are network engineers, senior engineers, change managers, CAB approvers, and auditors. One person may hold both the network engineer and the senior engineer role at the same time.

The resources are change requests and implementation records. Every change request records the engineer who requested it, the engineer who implemented it, the person who approved it, its assessed change risk, its affected-node count, its rollback-step count, its estimated cost, its change code, whether it is an emergency change, its change category, its current status, and its maintenance-window start. Every implementation record records the change it belongs to, who carried it out, and when it was carried out.

Each request carries the current time, whether it comes from the management network, whether a change-freeze waiver has been granted, and whether a major incident has been declared.

In this workflow a change is first approved and then implemented, and the implementation step can see the change's status, who approved it, and who implemented it as recorded by the approval step.

A change manager or CAB approver may approve a change only when their granted change-authority level is at least as high as the change's assessed risk, and a change whose risk exceeds the approver's authority may not be approved by that person.

This authority requirement is set aside when the change's estimated cost crosses the money threshold that requires CAB sign-off, in which case a CAB approver must sign off instead, and when the cost stays below that threshold the standard authority requirement applies.

A change may be implemented only after it has been approved, and a change that has not yet been approved may not be implemented.

The standard scheduling requirement is relaxed when the change is flagged as an emergency, allowing implementation ahead of the normal window, and when it is not flagged as an emergency the standard schedule applies.

Neither a network engineer nor a senior engineer may implement a change before it has been approved.

A run through the workflow by a change manager who approves a low-cost change within their authority and then has a network engineer implement it must be able to succeed.

The system manages telemetry access for an IoT and operational technology device fleet.

The people involved are operators, technicians, fleet admins, and service accounts. One person may hold both the operator and the technician role at the same time.

The resources are devices, telemetry, and commands. Every device records its owner, site group, firmware tags, maintenance mode, and status, and every telemetry record records its device and sensitivity.

Each requester carries their clearance and the groups they belong to.

An operator or fleet admin may read telemetry only when they belong under the device's site group.

An operator or fleet admin outside the device's site group must not read telemetry for that device.

An operator or fleet admin who does not own the device may read its telemetry only when their clearance is at least as high as the telemetry sensitivity.

An operator or fleet admin who owns the device may read its telemetry without meeting the telemetry sensitivity level, as long as they belong under the device's site group.

Neither an operator nor a fleet admin may read telemetry for a device outside their site group.

A request by an operator to read telemetry that does not trip any prohibition above must be able to succeed.

The system manages reading namespace secrets in Kubernetes namespaces.

The people involved are deployers, maintainers, cluster operators, and service accounts. One person may hold both the deployer and maintainer role at the same time.

The resources are namespaces, workloads, namespace secrets, and service account tokens. Every namespace secret records its namespace, owner, sensitivity, and status.

Each requester carries clearance, granted scope, and group membership.

Each request carries source IP, current time, emergency change, and whether MFA was used.

A deployer, maintainer, cluster operator, or service account may read a namespace secret only when their clearance is at least as high as the secret's sensitivity.

A deployer, maintainer, cluster operator, or service account with lower clearance than the secret's sensitivity must not read that secret.

A deployer, maintainer, cluster operator, or service account may read a namespace secret they own when no other rule blocks the request.

A deployer, maintainer, cluster operator, or service account must not read a namespace secret they do not own.

A deployer, maintainer, cluster operator, or service account may read a namespace secret only when the service account token presented for the request has not expired.

A deployer, maintainer, cluster operator, or service account must not read a namespace secret using an expired service account token.

A request by a deployer to read a namespace secret that does not trip any prohibition above must be able to succeed.

The system manages inpatient medical records and prescriptions.

The people involved are attending physicians, residents, nurses, and pharmacists.

One person may hold both the attending physician and pharmacist roles, or both the resident and pharmacist roles, at the same time.

The resources are medical records, prescriptions, and lab orders.

Every medical record records its patient, care team, ward, sensitivity, and status.

Every prescription records its patient, prescriber, and status.

Every lab order records its patient.

Each requester carries a cleared level and ward, and each request carries the current shift, whether an emergency has been declared, and whether multifactor authentication was used.

An attending physician, resident, or nurse may view a medical record only when the requester's cleared level is high enough for the record's sensitivity.

An attending physician, resident, or nurse whose cleared level is not high enough for the record's sensitivity must not view the medical record.

This clearance requirement applies to attending physicians, residents, and nurses when they request to view medical records.

The clearance requirement does not govern pharmacists because pharmacists are not one of the roles performing this view-record action.

The clearance requirement applies when the medical record is sealed.

When the medical record is not sealed, this sealed-record clearance requirement relaxes.

An attending physician, resident, or nurse must not view a sealed medical record whose sensitivity is above their cleared level.

A request by an attending physician to view a medical record that does not trip any prohibition above must be able to succeed.

This is the access-control document for the invoice approval and payment system.
The people involved are clerks, approvers, finance managers, and auditors, and one person may be both a clerk and an approver at the same time.
The resources are invoices, each recording their creator, approver, amount, surcharge, line-item count, status, cost center, and when they were submitted, and payments, each recording their invoice, issuer, and amount.
Each request carries the current time, whether the request is on the corporate network, and whether an emergency has been declared.
In this workflow the same invoice is first approved and then a payment is issued against it, and the payment step can see the invoice's status and who approved it as recorded by the approval step.
When an approver or a finance manager approves an invoice, it may be approved only after it has been submitted.
When a finance manager issues a payment, the person who approved the invoice may not be the one who issues its payment.
This approver-payer split is overridden when an emergency has been declared, in which case a finance manager may issue payment even on an invoice they themselves approved.
When no emergency has been declared, the person who approved an invoice may not issue its payment.
If the two rules on payment disagree, the declared emergency wins and the finance manager may issue the payment.
An approver or a finance manager must not approve an invoice that has not been submitted.
A finance manager must not issue payment on an invoice they themselves approved unless an emergency has been declared.
A run through the workflow by an approver that trips none of the prohibitions above must be able to succeed.

The system manages course modules and gradebook entries in a learning-management system.

The people involved are instructors of record, teaching assistants, learners, and coordinators. One person may hold both the instructor of record and teaching assistant roles at the same time.

The resources are modules and grade entries. Every module records its course, instructor of record, roster, prerequisite level, release time, locked setting, and status.

Every grade entry records its learner, module, who posted it, and its status.

Each requester carries their completed level.

Each request carries the current time, whether it is on the institution network, and the preview window.

An instructor of record or teaching assistant may enter a grade only while the grade entry is in draft status.

An instructor of record or teaching assistant must not enter a grade when the grade entry is not in draft status.

A person who is neither an instructor of record nor a teaching assistant must not enter a grade.

When the grade entry is in draft status, an instructor of record or teaching assistant may enter the grade if no other rule blocks the request.

A request by an instructor of record to enter a draft grade entry that trips no prohibition above must be able to succeed.

The system manages a continuous integration and deployment pipeline for a software company.

The people involved are committers, approvers, release managers, and site reliability engineers.

One person may hold both the committer and approver roles at the same time, and one person may hold both the approver and release manager roles at the same time.

The resources are deployments and artifacts.

Every deployment records its committer, its approver, its target environment, its change risk level, its artifact, and its status.

Every artifact records who built it, whether it has been signed, its build tags, and its status.

Each request to sign an artifact carries the current time, the source network address it was sent from, and whether it is an emergency change.

The committer who built an artifact must be the one who signs it.

A committer who did not build the artifact must not sign it, even if they are a committer, an approver, or a release manager on the same team.

An artifact may be signed only after its build has succeeded and its status shows as built.

An artifact may be signed only when it carries the "production-release" build tag.

An artifact may be signed only when the signing request comes from the corporate VPN network range.

A request by the committer who built a "production-release" artifact, whose build has succeeded, sent from the corporate VPN, to sign that artifact must be able to succeed.

The system manages the authorization and field execution of grid switching orders.

The people involved are planners, shift supervisors, operators, control-room operators, and auditors.

One person may hold both the planner and shift-supervisor roles, and one person may hold both the operator and control-room-operator roles.

The resources are switching orders and lockout tags.

Every switching order records the planner who prepared it, the operator designated to execute it, its feeder, its voltage level, its circuit count, its status, and its scheduled start and end times.

Every lockout tag records the order it belongs to, who applied it, and its feeder.

Each request carries the current time, whether it comes from the control-system network, whether lockout-tagout has been verified, and whether an outage emergency has been declared.

A planner or shift supervisor may authorize a switching order only while it is still in the planned state, and an order that has left the planned state may not be authorized.

An order may be authorized only when lockout-tagout has been verified in the control room beforehand, and may not be authorized while that verification is still outstanding.

When the order's voltage level is above the threshold that calls for shift-supervisor authorization, only a shift supervisor may authorize it, while at or below that voltage a planner may authorize it.

A request by a planner to authorize a switching order that breaks none of the rules above must be able to succeed.

This document describes how a source-code repository access system controls who may review a pull request and who may merge it.
The people involved are developers, reviewers, maintainers, and security leads, and one person may hold developer together with reviewer at the same time.
The resources are repositories, which record their owner, team, sensitivity, whether the default branch is protected, topics, and status; pull requests, which record their repository, author, who approved them, target branch, approval count, lines changed, whether a security review is required, and status; and branches, which record their name and whether they are protected.
In this workflow a pull request is first reviewed and then merged on the same pull request, and the merge step can see the pull request's status and who authored and approved it.
When a pull request is reviewed, a reviewer may not approve their own pull request.
That self-approval ban is set aside when the number of changed lines crosses the threshold requiring extra scrutiny, and it holds when the changed lines stay below that threshold.
The review step takes effect only when the person reviewing holds the designated role, and it does not take effect when they do not hold that role.
When a pull request is merged, the author of the pull request may not be the one who merges it.
A maintainer must not merge a pull request that they themselves authored.
A run through the workflow by a reviewer that trips none of these prohibitions must be able to succeed.

This system manages number portability authorization and cutover for a telephone carrier.

The people involved are porting specialists, porting supervisors, fraud reviewers, line technicians, and auditors. One person may hold both the porting specialist and fraud reviewer roles at the same time, and one person may hold both the line technician and porting specialist roles at the same time.

The resources are port requests and port completions. Every port request records who initiated it, who authorized it, the technician assigned to it, the account numbers being ported, the size of the number block, the gaining carrier code, the port type, the subscriber's region, its status, and the time it was requested. Every port completion records the request it belongs to, who completed the cutover, and the time the numbers were ported.

Each request carries the current time, whether it comes from the carrier's own operations network, whether a port-freeze override has been declared, and whether a regulator escalation is in effect.

The porting specialist who submitted a port request may not authorize that same request, to guard against a person slamming a port through on their own.

This bar does not apply when the account numbers being ported include a flagged or high-value line, in which case the specialist who submitted the request may authorize it.

When the account numbers include no flagged or high-value line, neither a porting specialist nor a porting supervisor may authorize a port request that they themselves submitted.

A request by a porting specialist who did not submit the port request to authorize it, tripping no prohibition above, must be able to succeed.

This document sets out who may approve grant awards and obligate their funds in the federal grant award management system.
The people involved are reviewers, program officers, grants officers, and applicants; one person may act as both a reviewer and a program officer, and one person may act as both a program officer and a grants officer.
The resources are applications, which record their applicant, assigned reviewers, funding tier, requested amount, program code, and status; and awards, which record their application, who approved them, who obligated their funds, their amount, whether they are flagged high risk, and their status.
Each request carries the current time, whether it comes from the government network, and whether an emergency has been declared.
In this workflow an award is first approved and then its funds are obligated, and the obligation step can see the award's status, who approved it, and who obligated it.
A program officer or grants officer may approve an award only when their approval authority is at or above the application's funding tier, and when their authority falls below that tier the approval must not proceed.
The grants officer who approved an award must not obligate its funds, so the obligation must fall to a different grants officer.
Funds may be obligated only when the requester holds the designated role, and when the requester lacks that role the obligation must not proceed.
A run through the workflow by a program officer that trips none of the prohibitions above must be able to succeed.

The system manages command delivery for an IoT and operational-technology device fleet.

The people involved are operators, technicians, fleet admins, and service accounts. One person may hold both the operator and technician role at the same time.

The resources are devices, telemetry, and commands. Every device records its owner, site group, firmware tags, maintenance mode, and status.

Each request carries its source IP address, current time, and maintenance window.

An operator, technician, or fleet admin may send a command only when the request falls within a permitted maintenance window.

Outside a permitted maintenance window, an operator, technician, or fleet admin must not send a command.

An operator, technician, or fleet admin may send a command to an active device.

An operator, technician, or fleet admin who does not own a device must not send a command to it when the device is provisioned or decommissioned.

An operator, technician, or fleet admin who owns a device may send a command to that device even when the device is provisioned or decommissioned, as long as the request is within a permitted maintenance window.

A request by an operator to send a command that does not trip any prohibition above must be able to succeed.

The system manages quality sign-off for manufacturing work orders before production release.

The people involved are operators, inspectors, quality managers, production supervisors, and auditors. One person may hold both the operator and inspector roles, and one person may hold both the inspector and quality manager roles.

The resources are work orders and production releases. Every work order records its operator, inspector, part code, defect count, hold flag, status, station, and creation time.

Each request carries the current time, whether it comes from the plant network, and whether a deviation has been authorized.

An operator may create a work order and start work on it.

An inspector or quality manager may sign off a work order only while it is in progress.

An inspector and a quality manager must not sign off a work order that is not in progress.

An inspector or quality manager may sign off a work order when the part code matches or has a controlled-part prefix.

An inspector and a quality manager must not sign off a work order when the part code neither matches nor has a controlled-part prefix.

An inspector or quality manager may sign off a work order when the recorded defect count is at or below the acceptance threshold.

An inspector and a quality manager must not sign off a work order when the recorded defect count is above the acceptance threshold.

A production supervisor may release a signed-off work order to production.

An auditor may view the quality log.

A request by an inspector to sign off an in-progress work order with an acceptable part code and a defect count at or below the acceptance threshold must be able to succeed.

The system manages immigration case adjudication and security-check clearance.

The people involved are adjudication officers, supervisory officers, background investigators, and records clerks. One person may hold both the adjudication officer and background investigator roles, and one person may hold both the supervisory officer and adjudication officer roles.

The resources are cases, security checks, and applicant records. Every case records its applicant, assigned officer, case team, field office, and status.

Every security check records its case, investigator, and status.

Every applicant record records its applicant, assigned officer, need-to-know team, data sensitivity, and status.

Each requester carries their clearance and recused cases.

Each request carries whether it is on the government network, the current time, and whether supervisor approval is present.

A background investigator may clear a security check only while it is pending.

A supervisory officer may clear a security check even when it is not pending.

A background investigator and a supervisory officer may clear a security check only during the permitted time window.

A background investigator and a supervisory officer must not clear a security check outside the permitted time window.

A request by a background investigator to clear a pending security check during the permitted time window, tripping no prohibition above, must be able to succeed.

The system manages access to source-code repositories, their pull requests, and their branches for a software engineering organization.

The people involved are developers, reviewers, maintainers, and security leads.

One person may hold both the developer and reviewer role at the same time.

The resources are repositories, pull requests, and branches.

Every repository records its owner, team, sensitivity classification, whether its default branch is protected, its topic tags, and its lifecycle status.

Every pull request records its repository, author, approvers, target branch, approval count, lines changed, whether it requires security review, and its status.

Every branch records its name and whether it is protected.

Each requester carries a clearance level of public, internal, confidential, or restricted, in ascending order of access.

To clone a repository, the requester's clearance level must be at least as high as the repository's sensitivity classification.

A developer, reviewer, maintainer, or security lead must not clone a repository whose sensitivity classification is higher than their own clearance level.

Cloning is only permitted when the repository carries the "regulated-data" topic tag.

A repository that does not carry the "regulated-data" tag may be cloned without this clearance check applying.

Cloning is only permitted when the repository's lifecycle status is active.

A repository that has been archived may not be cloned, even by a requester whose clearance is otherwise sufficient.

A request by a developer with confidential clearance to clone an active repository tagged "regulated-data" and classified as confidential must be able to succeed.

The system manages advertising campaigns and their creatives in a marketing platform.

The people involved are advertisers, account managers, brand safety reviewers, and campaign directors. One person may hold both the account-manager and the campaign-director role at the same time.

The resources are campaigns and creatives. Every campaign records its advertiser, who prepared it, its budget, its contingency, its budget tier, its risk labels, its scheduled start, and its status.

Each request carries the current time, whether multi-factor authentication was used, whether the device is trusted, and whether an emergency launch is declared.

In this workflow a campaign's budget is first approved and then the campaign is launched, and the launch step can see the campaign's status and who prepared it as recorded by the approval step.

An account manager or campaign director who prepared a campaign may not approve its budget when its budget plus contingency crosses the threshold, and for a budget plus contingency at or below the threshold the preparer may approve it.

A budget may be approved only when multi-factor authentication was used, and a request to approve one without multi-factor authentication is refused.

A campaign may be launched only after its budget has been approved, and a request to launch one whose budget is not yet approved is refused.

A campaign may be launched only by its owning advertiser, and an account manager or campaign director who is not the owning advertiser may not launch it.

A campaign may be launched only when it carries the required risk label, and a request to launch one without that label is refused.

A run through the workflow in which a campaign director who did not prepare a campaign approves its budget with multi-factor authentication and the owning advertiser then launches the campaign carrying the required risk label, tripping no prohibition above, must be able to succeed.

The system manages deployment approvals in a CI/CD pipeline.

The people involved are committers, approvers, release managers, and SREs. One person may hold both the committer and approver roles, or both the approver and release manager roles, at the same time.

The resources are deployments and artifacts. Every deployment records its committer, approver, target environment, change risk, artifact, and status.

Every artifact records who built it, whether it is signed, its build tags, and its status.

Each requester carries a deploy tier.

Each request carries the current time, source IP, and whether the change is an emergency change.

An approver or release manager may approve a deployment.

An approver who committed a deployment must not approve it.

A release manager who committed a deployment must not approve it.

When a deployment's change-risk score crosses the extra-scrutiny threshold, an approver or release manager may approve it only after it has been submitted for review.

When a deployment's change-risk score does not cross the extra-scrutiny threshold, the submitted-for-review requirement does not block approval.

A request by an approver to approve a deployment that does not trip any prohibition above must be able to succeed.
